sasha: quick heads-up — a canary run surfaced periodic p99 spikes (~180–250ms) for streamed responses that are ~8–16 tokens. Looks like 'microflush' interactions with kernel selection and partial-decode scheduling. posting profiling excerpt below.

kevin: do you have the perf traces? p99 for what metric — end-to-end latency or kernel launch?

sasha: end-to-end server-side latency (request->first-stream chunk). kernel launch + small-batch inefficiencies are visible. snippet from the perf trace (flattened):
```
TIME  EVENT                             LAT(ms)
0.00  enqueue request                    0.2
0.40  decide batch                       1.8
2.20  schedule kernel A (small-kernel)   0.6
2.90  partial decode (emit 8 tokens)     12.4
15.30 kernel switch -> kernel B          37.8  <-- big jump
53.10 KV lookup/handoff                   3.1
56.20 emit chunk -> flush                0.8
57.00 total -> first-chunk lat           57.0 (p50)
200.8                                  200.8 (p99 spike)
```

maria: interesting — that kernel switch at ~37ms looks like the culprit. can we avoid selecting kernel B for short sequential decodes? what's the kernel selection heuristic right now?

kevin: today we pick kernel based on (seq_len_bucket, model_layer_cfg, quant_profile). seq_len_bucket is coarse: [<=8, <=64, <=256, >256]. maybe our heuristic misclassifies streamed partial decodes because they start small then grow, so we reselect mid-request.

tom: exactly — partial-decode scheduling is causing the runtime to re-evaluate kernel choice mid-inference when cached KV grows. kernel B is optimized for longer sequences and uses a different launch config that has higher setup cost. so for streams that will likely stay short, the setup cost dominates.

sasha: KV cache behavior also contributes — small responses that hit cache still trigger the re-eval path because the batcher combines requests with different KV staleness. when that happens, the runtime falls back to the safest kernel (B) which causes the spike.

maria: proposal: add a 'microflush-aware kernel pin' policy: if a request emitted <=X tokens during the first Y steps and batch expected remaining tokens <=Z, keep initial kernel choice for N more decode steps. defaults: X=8, Y=2, Z=32, N=4.

kevin: +1. also try increasing stream_flush_min_bytes/tokens to reduce frequent microflushes. example config we could AB test: 
```
continuous_batching: {
  min_batch_tokens: 64,
  max_batch_tokens: 2048,
  stream_flush_min_tokens: 32,   # was 8
  microflush_pin_steps: 4,
  kernel_pin_policy: "early"  # prefer earlier kernel for short-lived decodes
}
```

tom: runbook note: when enabling kernel_pin_policy, watch for any regressed long-seq throughput. kernel B is still better for long sequences. we should gate by model size / layer dims.

sasha: i've run a quick synthetic canary: enabling microflush pin + stream_flush_min_tokens=32 reduced p99 spikes in this workload from 210ms -> 65ms (sample of 10k requests, client-side p99-first-chunk). p50 unaffected.

maria: nice. schedule: small canary across 5% of traffic in eu-west1, collect p50/p95/p99 for first-chunk and total-req. also track kernel-switch counts and KV stall rate.

kevin: add a prometheus metric: runtime_kernel_switches_total{reason="mid_decode_reselect"}. compare pre/post.

infra-bot: deploybot: canary rollout started for feature-flag 'microflush_kernel_pin' -> channels: canary-eu-west1 -> 5% at 2026-03-17T14:47:25Z

sasha: cool — i'll own the experiment and collect traces. next steps: (1) run 48h canary, (2) gather kernel_switches & p99-first-chunk, (3) if p99 drops and long-seq throughput delta <2%, propose global rollout.

maria: if stats look good, we should add an automated heuristic to lower stream_flush_min_tokens for model families where kernel B is strictly better (i.e., don't pin).

kevin: nice concise plan. tagging infra for observability dashboards and eng-sre for alert thresholds.

sasha: thanks — i'll post the canary dashboard link when ready and attach full traces. :thumbsup:
